In And Circumcenter B

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: Move a triangle and watch two lines inside it: they always cross at a right angle, and sometimes they are the same length too. There is nothing to win.
How to play: Drag A, B or C, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes for names, equal-length marks, helper lines and the right-angle mark; press Reset to start over.

Drag a corner, or focus it and press the arrow keys (Shift for bigger steps).

Look for the math

Drag a corner and the two coloured lines turn together. They always cross squarely; making one corner a particular size also makes the lines exactly the same length. That is the bundled statement on the original page.

The two lines to compare

Lay the side AB off along the other two sides: D sits on the ray from B through C with BD = AB, and E sits on the ray from A through C with AE = AB. The blue dot I is the incenter, where the angle bisectors meet; the red dot O is the centre of the circumcircle through all three corners. The lines to compare are DE and IO. The logic test rebuilt both centres exactly as the applet does and matched them on more than four thousand triangles.

Why they are always square

Extend the angle bisector AI until it meets the circumcircle again at F. Since AB = AE, the line AI is the perpendicular bisector of BE: M is the midpoint of BE and FB = FE. An inscribed angle on the chord AB gives ∠BFE = 2∠C, and the page's proof also shows BF = IF. Turning both arms of ∠IFO by a quarter turn gives ∠DBE, so IO must be at right angles to DE. Over the grid and random sample the largest absolute cosine between the two lines was below 1e-8: the page's "independent of C" claim holds.

The extra equality

A chord of length AB in a circle of radius R gives AB = 2R sin(C). At C = 30° this makes R = AB, so OF = OA = AB = BD. With IF = BE the triangles IFO and BDE agree by side-angle-side, hence IO = DE. The test checked the stronger formula DE = 2·IO·sin(C) everywhere: it gives equality at 30°, and also at 150° because sin(150°) = sin(30°) — a case the page does not mention.

Drag C towards the top-left until the status says about 30°, then tick Equal lengths, Hint and Right angle to watch F, M and the square corner appear.
